summary: This script queries an AnythingLLM AI workspace about blog articles, displays the AI's answer along with cited sources as clickable links, then performs a secondary exact-match search through blog frontmatter to find additional relevant articles the AI might have missed. It filters out common words and overly-frequent terms to surface genuinely topical matches.

explanations.10: These three lines make the script exit immediately if any command fails, if you use an undefined variable, or if a pipe contains any failed command — this prevents silent errors from cascading.
explanations.14: This sets a default workspace name to 'blog' unless the environment variable ANYTHINGLLM_WORKSPACE was already defined elsewhere.
explanations.16: This checks if the user provided any arguments; if they didn't, we show usage instructions and exit.
explanations.20: The question is everything the user typed after the command name — '$*' joins all arguments into one string.
explanations.23: This tries to load the API key from an environment variable first; if that's empty and a .env file exists, it reads the key from that file instead.
explanations.26: This is a bash idiom that says 'use this variable if it exists, otherwise fail with this error message' — it's a guard that prevents the script from running without proper credentials.
explanations.29: The script tries two different network addresses where AnythingLLM might be running (localhost, or the Docker host gateway IP), testing each one to see which responds.
explanations.45: The curl command sends an HTTP POST request to the AI with our question; the response (which will be JSON) gets stored in a variable.
explanations.49: jq generates JSON from scratch: it takes the user's question as the 'm' variable and a unique session ID (built from random numbers and the process ID) as the 's' variable, then wraps them in a JSON object.
explanations.52: After the response arrives, we extract any error message from the JSON (or get nothing if there's no error field), then check if one exists.
explanations.58: This prints the original question in cyan and bold, with a question-mark emoji, followed by two blank lines.
explanations.63: The '-t 1' test checks if output is connected to a terminal (not piped to a file); this determines whether to use fancy clickable links or plain URLs.
explanations.65: This creates clickable hyperlinks using ANSI OSC 8 codes — the URL becomes clickable text in VS Code and Windows Terminal.
explanations.74: This jq filter extracts sources from the AI response: it finds items where the source looks like a web link, renames and reshapes them, removes duplicates, then outputs them as tab-separated URL and title pairs.
explanations.82: The 'IFS=$'\t'' sets the field separator to a tab character, so when reading each source line, the URL and title split into separate variables.
explanations.112: This takes the user's question, converts it to individual words (one per line), removes punctuation, lowercases everything, keeps only words 4+ characters long, and deduplicates them.
explanations.114: This filters out all the stopwords (like 'the', 'what', 'docker') by comparing each candidate word against a list and rejecting matches.
explanations.120: The ceiling is one-tenth of the total article count, but never less than 3 — this prevents common words from matching too many articles and drowning out specific results.
explanations.126: This searches blog article metadata files for each keyword, counting how many articles mention it; if a word appears in too many articles (beyond the ceiling), it's skipped as too common.
explanations.141: sed extracts the 'slug' field from the YAML frontmatter (the URL-friendly name of the article), then removes surrounding quotes if present.
explanations.143: This prints the constructed blog URL using the slug, making another clickable link to the matched article.
